column11: FIONA's own design paper puts the prevalence of CKD in children at 30 to 100 per million age-related population (Trials 2024, doi:10.1186/s13063-024-08021-z, PMC10956186, introduction), applied to the 73,132,720 US residents under 18 on 1 July 2024 (US Census Bureau Vintage 2024 national population estimates by age and sex, file nc-est2024-agesex-res, the denominator the book's paediatric rows use). The top of the range is taken: 73.13 x 100 = 7,313 children
column12: a range of 3.3-fold, and the top end is taken for two reasons. The national studies behind it count CKD stages 2 to 5, while FIONA also admits stage 1 with a UPCR of 1.0 g/g or more, which those counts leave out. And they are mostly hospital-based European series, which find the patients already in nephrology care. The bottom end, 30 per million, would give 2,194

column11: the share of children with CKD stages 2 to 3b whose proteinuria reaches FIONA's threshold of a UPCR of 0.5 g/g or more. In the CKiD cohort (599 children aged 6 months to 16 with an eGFR of 30 to 90, the eGFR range FIONA enrols), baseline UPCR was a median 0.33 mg/mg, interquartile range 0.12 to 0.95 (Greenberg et al., J Am Soc Nephrol 2025;36:1105-1115, doi:10.1681/ASN.0000000602, PMC12147970). 0.5 lies between the median and the upper quartile; interpolated on the log scale it is the 59.8th percentile, so 40.2% are above it. 7,313 x 0.402 = about 2,940 children
column12: the interpolation is mine and the row's weakest step: the distribution is read from three quantiles, not counted. FIONA also requires an optimised ACE inhibitor or ARB, which is not taken off because proteinuric children in nephrology care are mostly on one already, and excludes stage 4 and 5, which the prevalence counts and this share partly removes since CKiD stops at an eGFR of 30

column11: a judgement. The case for: an ACE inhibitor or ARB is the only therapy shown to lower proteinuria in children (FIONA design paper, Trials 2024), and SGLT2 inhibitors have not been studied in children with CKD (both from the same paper). The case against: paediatric nephrologists will add a second potassium-raising agent cautiously in children prone to dehydration, and the label would come on a proteinuria surrogate rather than a kidney outcome. The design paper expects enrolment to lean to immune-mediated glomerular disease with treatment-refractory proteinuria, a narrower group than the pool
